extracted.intended_audience: students, mathematicians, and general readers interested in mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for producing and understanding mathematical proofs: what counts as a proof, required properties (deduction, exhaustiveness, axiomatic basis), common proof methods, presentation conventions, and verification concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: deductive argument guaranteeing conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof is a deductive argument for a mathematical statement, showing that the stated assumptions logically guarantee the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument may use other previously established statements, such as theorems; but every proof can, in principle, be constructed using only certain basic or original assumptions known as axioms, along with the accepted rules of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic basis and rules of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proof can, in principle, be constructed using only certain basic or original assumptions known as axioms, along with the accepted rules of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows proofs to be formalized; modern proof theory treats proofs as inductively defined data structures based on chosen axioms (e.g., ZFC, non-Euclidean axioms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive deductive reasoning (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are examples of exhaustive deductive reasoning that establish logical certainty, to be distinguished from empirical arguments or non-exhaustive inductive reasoning that establish 'reasonable expectation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting many cases in which the statement holds is not enough for a proof, which must demonstrate that the statement is true in all possible cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of previously established results
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may use other previously established statements, such as theorems, lemmas, and definitions as part of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to rely on known results, provided their use is legitimate within the chosen axiomatic framework and is properly referenced or proven earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal vs informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are often written in terms of rigorous informal logic; purely formal proofs are written fully in symbolic language without natural language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal proof is a sequence of formulas in a formal language starting with assumptions and each subsequent formula a logical consequence of preceding ones. While most published proofs are informal, they should be convertible in principle into formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal standards of rigor and audience adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of rigor is not absolute and has varied throughout history; a proof can be presented differently depending on the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To gain acceptance, a proof has to meet communal standards of rigor; an argument considered vague or incomplete may be rejected. Presentation should match audience expectations for rigor and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and avoidance of ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs employ logic expressed in mathematical symbols, along with natural language that usually admits some ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because natural language can be ambiguous, proofs should strive for rigor and clarity; ambiguous or incomplete natural-language arguments risk rejection or misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: In direct proof, the conclusion is established by logically combining the axioms, definitions, and earlier theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving sum of two even integers is even by expressing each as 2a and 2b and showing their sum is 2(a+b). Use definitions and basic properties (closure, distributive law) to derive conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by mathematical induction (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: In proof by mathematical induction, a single 'base case' is proved, and an 'induction rule' is proved that establishes that any arbitrary case implies the next case; thus all cases follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants include proof by infinite descent. Useful to avoid proving infinitely many individual cases; explicitly state base case and induction step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contraposition (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contraposition infers 'if p then q' by establishing the logically equivalent contrapositive: 'if not q then not p'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when contrapositive is easier to prove than the original implication (example: if x^2 is even then x is even).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction / reductio ad absurdum (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the statement is true (or assume negation), derive a logical contradiction, and hence conclude the statement (or its negation) must be false (or true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous example: irrationality of sqrt(2). Often used for existence or non-existence proofs; be careful about hidden assumptions in the contradiction argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by construction (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive proof (proof by construction) demonstrates existence by constructing a concrete example with the desired property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to give explicit examples (e.g., Liouville's explicit transcendental numbers). Also used to produce counterexamples to disprove universal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by exhaustion (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the conclusion by dividing it into a finite number of cases and proving each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of cases can be very large; computer checking of many cases (e.g., the four color theorem) is accepted but sometimes controversial; be explicit about case partitioning and verification method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed chain inference (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a collection of statements are pairwise equivalent by proving implications in a cycle: φ1⇒φ2, φ2⇒φ3, …, φn⇒φ1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitivity of implication to conclude pairwise equivalence; ensure each implication is proven clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic proof / probabilistic method (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use probability to show that an object with a given property exists by proving a non-zero probability of selecting such an object from a large set of candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method shows existence without identifying a particular object; distinguish probabilistic proof from mere plausibility arguments; some probabilistic algorithms (e.g., primality testing) approach the epistemic status of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish equivalence of expressions by showing they count the same object in different ways, often via a bijection or double counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit bijections or counting arguments to demonstrate equality of combinatorial expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconstructive proof (method and distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that a mathematical object with a certain property exists without explaining how such an object can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often implemented via contradiction; contrast with constructive proofs which provide a method to find the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical proofs / statistical proof using data (terminology and caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'statistical proof' may be used technically or colloquially in some areas of pure mathematics (cryptography, probabilistic number theory) or to refer to proofs in mathematical statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: statistical evidence or computational/empirical observations are not substitutes for deductive proof; clarify context when using this terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted proofs (verification concerns and practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated theorem provers and proof assistants are used to prove theorems and carry out calculations too long for humans to check; some proofs rely on computer-checked case analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about program or runtime errors mean one should reduce error risk via redundancy, self-checks, multiple independent approaches and programs; rigorous formalization in proof assistants increases confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on axioms and undecidability
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement that is neither provable nor disprovable from a set of axioms is called undecidable (from those axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the axiomatic system in use (e.g., ZFC); recognize that provability can depend on chosen axioms and that some statements may be independent of those axioms (Gödel incompleteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation conventions: ending a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for indicating the end of a proof include writing 'Q.E.D.' (quod erat demonstrandum) or using a square/tombstone symbol (□ or ∎, 'Halmos').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the end symbol verbally in oral presentations if desired; Unicode provides an 'end of proof' character U+220E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational/formal formats: two-column proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-column proof organizes statements and reasons side-by-side: left column holds propositions, right column holds brief explanations (axiom, hypothesis, derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in elementary geometry instruction; use for pedagogy to make logical flow explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criterion: mathematical beauty and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may be admired for their mathematical beauty; elegance is a valued (though subjective) attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While beauty is not a formal requirement, elegant or insightful proofs (e.g., those Paul Erdős described as from 'The Book') are often prized and can guide mathematicians toward deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual proofs use pictures or geometric/diagrammatic reasoning to make an argument convincing or suggestive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual or heuristic devices can provide plausibility and insight but should be supplemented by rigorous justification when a formal proof is required.
